newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD vows to block coalition tax reform.
newsitem.headline: German SPD vows to block coalition tax reform.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Friday the ruling centre-right coalition's latest tax reform proposals still fell short of the mark and vowed to block them with its majority in the upper house of parliament.

Industry groups and trade unions also criticised the amended tax reforms agreed on Thursday by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition to fill new gaps in the 1998 and 1999 budgets. The reforms are to be put to the Bundestag (lower house) on June 26 in a bill.

Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) welcomed the deal struck with their liberal Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners, but some outspoken regional CDU leaders warned Bonn that if the coalition were not more flexible in future this could spell its collapse.

SPD parliamentary leader Peter Struck told Inforadio in Berlin his party remained firmly opposed to the coalition's plans to introduce tax increases on pay for weekend and evening shiftwork, even though this would now be done in stages instead of at one blow.
"The coalition has shown some willingness to compromise on taxes for weekend and night shift bonus pay," Struck said. "But that does not go far enough."
Struck said the SPD also rejected the coalition's unchanged insistence on trimming tax breaks for commuters.
SPD deputy parliamentary leader Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier said the party would not approve the reforms unless it was clear how the package would be financed.
The Association of Wholesalers and Exporters (BGA) also said the coalition's latest proposals were ill-conceived.

BGA president Michael Fuchs said the coalition was wrong to propose gradual tax hikes on weekend and night shift work and an introduction of limits on the losses corporations could carry forward to offset future profits.

"The business sector already pays a disproportionate share to raise state revenue and should not be asked to pay more," Fuchs said in a statement. He also said coalition plans to abolish a tax break on imported goods would hit importers hard.

Walter Riester, deputy president of Germany's largest union IG Metall, told Suedwestfunk radio his union was firmly opposed to phased-in taxation of night and weekend shiftwork and argued this still failed to solve Bonn's budgetary impasse.
Members of Kohl's CDU/FDP coalition, teetering on the brink of collapse over how to fill a 19 billion mark ($11 billion) budget gap this year, welcomed Thursday's agreement.
Deputy CDU parliamentary leader Heiner Geissler said the amended plan, a mixture of eliminating tax write-offs and lowering tax rates, would raise an extra three billion marks.

The reforms, which aim to lower tax rates for companies and individuals while making it more difficult to avoid taxes, were originally intended to reduce the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks in 1999. But it was unclear if the amended plan would hit that target.
Members of a group of up-and-coming CDU regional leaders, dubbed by the German media the "young wild ones", warned the Bonn coalition inflexibility could mean its demise.
Peter Mueller, CDU leader in the state of Saar, blamed Bonn's budgetary impasse on the FDP junior coalition partners, Germany's self-styled party of tax-cutters.

Mueller also blamed Finance Minister Theo Waigel, saying he should drop his insistence on a strict interpretation of financial criteria for countries to qualify for the planned 1999 launch of Europe's planned single currency, the euro.
